title: Characteristic Classes: Curvature, Roots, And Classifying Examples
notes: Open by framing characteristic classes as a routing problem for bundles. The chapter span is short, so the lecture is not a catalog of every construction. It gives students one mental model: local geometric choices produce global cohomology classes, and those classes become computable when we move between curvature, projectivization, roots, and universal examples.

title: The Chapter's Organizing Question
notes: Use this slide to slow down the vocabulary. A vector bundle can look locally trivial everywhere, so the question is how to record the failure of one global trivialization. Characteristic classes are the answer, but each family chooses a coefficient system and a geometric test. Keep the four verbs visible: detect, represent, pull back, compute.

title: Four Families, Four Coefficient Habits
notes: The table prevents a common confusion: Euler, Stiefel-Whitney, Chern, and Pontrjagin classes are not interchangeable labels. They live in different coefficient worlds and answer slightly different obstruction questions. Stiefel-Whitney classes are mod 2, Chern classes see complex structure, Pontrjagin classes turn real bundles through complexification, and Euler classes need orientation.

title: Chern-Weil Intuition
notes: Even though the chapter develops Chern classes through projectivization and splitting, the course is about differential forms, so students need the Chern-Weil picture in the background. A connection has curvature. Invariant polynomials in curvature are closed forms. Changing the connection changes the representative, not the cohomology class. That is the de Rham intuition.

title: Euler Class: A Top Obstruction
notes: Present the Euler class as the most geometric member of the family. For an oriented real rank n bundle, a generic section vanishes in codimension n, and the signed zero locus represents the top obstruction. In de Rham language the Pfaffian curvature form is a representative. The point is not the formula but the obstruction story.

title: Stiefel-Whitney Classes: Mod 2 Obstructions
notes: Stiefel-Whitney classes are included because they are part of the characteristic-class landscape, even though they do not fit directly into de Rham coefficients. Emphasize the first two tests: w1 detects orientability, while w2 measures the next lifting obstruction in many geometric settings. The mod 2 coefficient system removes signs and preserves real-bundle information.

title: Chern Classes From Projectivization
notes: Now enter the chapter's main construction. Instead of starting with curvature forms, the text uses the projectivized bundle and its tautological line. The class x equals the first Chern class of the dual tautological line. Leray-Hirsch says powers of x form a basis over the base, so the one relation defines the Chern classes.

title: Splitting Principle As Proof Transport
notes: The splitting principle is the slide where students often need reassurance. It does not claim that the original bundle splits on the original base. It says we may pull back to a flag bundle where the pullback splits, and because cohomology pulls back injectively, any polynomial identity verified upstairs descends downstairs.

title: Chern Root Algebra
notes: Use the root notation as a computational grammar rather than a new kind of object. Once E behaves like a sum of line bundles, c of E becomes the product of one plus each root. Whitney products, dual signs, line twists, exterior powers, and top-class tests all become symmetric polynomial identities. The notebook checks these identities exactly.

title: Pontrjagin Classes From Complexification
notes: Pontrjagin classes are the real-bundle family that becomes visible after complexification. The paired roots u and negative u, v and negative v explain why odd Chern classes vanish in the de Rham model. The even Chern classes remain, with the usual sign convention, and those are repackaged as p1, p2, and so on.

title: How The Families Talk To Each Other
notes: This slide is a comparison map, not a proof of every relation. The important teaching move is to ask what structure has been forgotten or added. A complex bundle has an underlying real bundle. An oriented real plane bundle can be treated like a complex line after choosing compatible structure. Reducing integral information mod 2 changes what can be detected.

title: Classifying Examples
notes: Examples keep the lecture from becoming purely formal. The tautological line over projective space supplies the generator students can actually compute with. Trivial bundles kill all positive characteristic classes. Tangent bundles and oriented plane bundles show why the top class has geometric content. These examples also prepare the classifying-space slide that follows.

title: Universal Bundle Lens
notes: The classifying-space lens explains why characteristic classes are natural. A bundle is pulled back from a universal bundle over BG, and its classes are pulled back from universal cohomology classes. This is the cleanest way to understand why formulas verified for universal examples control all bundles of the same structure group.

title: Chapter Checklist
notes: Close with a checklist students can reuse. Before computing a characteristic class, name the bundle structure, choose coefficients, decide whether a curvature or topological model is being used, move to roots only through a justified splitting argument, and test examples. That habit turns a dense chapter into a sequence of controlled choices.
